extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history / journalism/media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practices for producing and evaluating 1830s 'penny press' newspapers — their editorial choices, business models, reporting techniques, and ethical tradeoffs. The page discusses what made papers like the New York Sun and Herald succeed and how they were criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, readable news copy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun appeared ... The paper was neat, the type small, the news concisely stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, tightly written items and small type-pages made the paper readable and portable; prefer brevity over long, heavy treatments that characterized six-cent papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on local, human-interest, and sensational events
rubrics_metrics.description: The fresh, even flippant, style of the Sun’s news items, and its emphasis on local, human-interest, and often sensational events caught the town’s fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize items that are immediate, local, and emotionally engaging (crime, petty drama, curiosities). This editorial focus was a deliberate circulation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of police-court reporting as entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Sun features which made it immediately popular was its police-court report. The humorous treatment of police-court news ... amusement of drunkenness, theft, assaults, and street-walking had hoisted the circulation ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform routine court proceedings into readable, often humorous vignettes; effective for circulation but can be crude, exploitative, or ethically questionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Print whatever was interesting and readable’ editorial principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun broke sharply with the traditional American news concept, and began to print whatever was interesting and readable regardless of its wide significance or recognized importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reader interest and readability over claims of objective importance; this drives news selection but may subordinate civic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-price circulation model and street vendor system (the 'London plan')
rubrics_metrics.description: The one-cent price brought a circulation ... Day sent newsboys on the street to cry his paper. Since he charged the boys only sixty-seven cents a hundred if they paid cash ... he soon had his street sales on a cash-in-advance basis; the boys collected six cents a week from the subscribers on their regular routes. This was known as 'the London plan' of circulation management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use low cover price plus aggressive street sales to maximize distribution; provide favorable wholesale terms to newsboys to ensure cash-in-advance sales and routine collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business investment in presses, equipment, and scale to support growth
rubrics_metrics.description: On the business side Day ... installed one of the new Napier presses and enlarged the size of its pages. ... The Beaches provided the Sun with the best presses and equipment ... it kept to one cent when its leading rivals ... raised their price to two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in faster presses, larger pages, and mechanical improvements to increase output, lower marginal cost, and expand circulation; technical investment underpins editorial and commercial ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensational hoaxes and fabricated stories as circulation tools (with credibility risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Late in August, 1835, the Sun printed ... a series about 'Herschel discoveries' culminating in the man-bat inhabitants of the satellite. Locke’s moon hoax ... aroused interest ... Locke confided ... that he had written the entire series out of whole cloth; ... other papers turned upon the Sun with criticism for the falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabricated sensational narratives can massively boost readership in short term but risk exposure, criticism, and long-term damage to credibility; consider ethical and reputational costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content mix: serial stories, theatrical notices, and accessible features
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun had an abundance of short, breezy items, with some theatrical notices, paragraphs about monstrosities and prodigies, and an emphasis on crime news. ... Its serial stories were a prominent feature; Mary Jane Holmes and Horatio Alger, Jr., amused its readers with sentimental romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine short news items, serialized fiction, theater chit-chat, and spectacle items to keep readers engaged across issues; tailoring content to audience tastes increases loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff: low price clienteles affect advertising quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Its low price ... caused it to find its clientele among the poorer classes. This in turn brought it a lower class of advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that targeting lower-price mass markets will shape the advertiser base; editorial and commercial strategies must balance revenue from ads with audience composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between objective reporting and editorializing/personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything was personalized. Wit supplanted dignity; recklessness took the place of conservatism. Objective reporting suffered and news reports were editorialized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalized, witty presentation can attract readers but risks undermining objectivity and credibility; editors must balance spice with factual rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Populist editorial voice: 'be with the people' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor must always be with the people— think with them— feel with them— and he need fear nothing, he will always be right— always be strong— always popular— always free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a populist, accessible editorial stance that aligns with common sentiments; effective for building readership but can lead to demagoguery or loss of editorial distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust financial/market reporting as a distinct product
rubrics_metrics.description: Wall Street reports more thorough and candid than any New York had ever known. His first 'money article' ... became an established institution; it was the forerunner of the modern financial page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop comprehensive, trustworthy financial coverage (money articles) to attract business readers and institutional subscribers; this requires expertise and can differentiate a paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extensive verbatim trial reporting and crime-detailing
rubrics_metrics.description: He built up the Robinson-Jewett murder trial ... Verbatim reports of the testimony were given, with questions and answers. It was a great field-day for the penny press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing verbatim testimony and exhaustive trial coverage can captivate readers but raises privacy, taste, and sensationalism concerns; editorial discretion advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society coverage and the rise of society pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Another type of news which made readers for the Herald was that of Society ... Stories of expensive parties ... were always spiced by a hit of satire. So ciety was at first aghast, then amused, then complacent, and finally hungry for penny-press-stories of its own — such were the origins of the modern society page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover high-society events with a mix of reportage and satirical commentary to attract readers interested in social life; this can evolve into a lucrative regular feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor self-promotion and personality-selling
rubrics_metrics.description: Bennett believed in advertising himself— 'selling' his own personality to the public. He compared himself with Napoleon, with Moses. ... When the editor used the same blatancy in regard to his own marriage, many were disgusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing the editor’s persona may increase readership and brand distinctiveness but risks alienating more fastidious readers and appearing in poor taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in news-gathering infrastructure to beat rivals
rubrics_metrics.description: He was soon claiming ... he set up a European correspondence, set up a Washington bureau, procure his own correspondents in the leading American cities, and buy a small fleet of boats to outstrip his rivals in meeting the news-bearing vessels from abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build correspondent networks, bureaus, and rapid distribution methods (boats, presses) to secure exclusives and faster incoming news; such investments support long-term competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste, decorum, and moral criticism risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainly there was reason for criticism of the Herald. It exploited crime news. It seemed to delight in stories of illicit sex relations— scandalous incidents recounted without names, some of them probably more or less fictitious. It shocked many readers by criticism of the revival meetings of the times, and it was often disrespectful of the church and church leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect moral and taste-based pushback when publishing salacious, irreverent, or disrespectful content; weigh short-term gains against reputational and institutional backlash.
